# Styling {#chp:style}

::: epigraph
> It's not just what it looks like and feels like. Design is how it works.
>
> ---Steve Jobs, as quoted in *The New York Times Magazine* (2003)
:::

The default look of an **lt** table is deliberately plain: a rule on top, a rule
below the header, a rule at the bottom, and nothing else. It is a good canvas.
This chapter is about the three functions that let you paint on it:
`lt_style()` for individual cells, `lt_css()` for rules that apply to the whole
table, and `lt_wrap()` for keeping those rules from leaking into other tables on
the same page.

## Paint a few cells {#sec:style-cells}

Start with the shortcuts. `lt_style()` takes the columns and rows to hit, and
then a handful of arguments you would otherwise have to spell in CSS: `bold`,
`italic`, `color`, and `bg`. Leave `columns` out to cover every column, and leave
`rows` out to cover every row.

```{r}
lt(head(mtcars[, 1:4], 5)) |>
  lt_style(~ mpg, rows = 1, bold = TRUE, color = "#06c") |>
  lt_style(rows = 5, italic = TRUE, bg = "#fff3cd")
```

Anything else goes in the dots. Write the property name in camelCase
(`borderBottom`) or as a quoted dash-case name (`` `border-bottom` ``), with the
value as a string. Those are plain CSS properties, so you can reach for whatever
the browser supports:

```{r}
lt(head(mtcars[, 1:4], 4)) |>
  lt_style(~ mpg, rows = 1, borderBottom = "2px solid crimson", letterSpacing = ".1em")
```

## Let the data pick the cells {#sec:style-test}

Hard-coding row numbers works until the data changes. A better habit is to say
*what* should be highlighted and let the table find it. Pass `test`, a small
JavaScript function that receives the raw value of each cell and returns `true`
for the cells that deserve the style.

The example below does exactly that. It also shows the second trick: instead of
inline styles, tag matching cells with a `class` and write the rules once with
`lt_css()`. The table then carries a class name per cell instead of a copy of the
style, which keeps the output small.

```{r, child = ex('style')}
```

::: {.callout-note data-legend="Why JavaScript?"}
The test runs in the browser, not in R. That is what lets the highlighting
survive sorting, filtering, and paging in an interactive table (@chp:interactive):
the table re-evaluates the test whenever the rows move. The price is that `test`
is a string of JavaScript, not an R expression, and it sees the *raw* value, so
`v < 0.05` compares numbers even if the cell shows `"<0.05"` after formatting.
:::

A missing value arrives in the test as `null`, which makes it easy to flag the
holes in your data:

```{r}
d = data.frame(Site = c("A", "B", "C"), Enrolled = c(120, NA, 87))
lt(d) |>
  lt_style(~ Enrolled, test = "v => v == null", bg = "#fde2e2") |>
  lt_style(~ Enrolled, test = "v => v > 100", bold = TRUE)
```

By default `NA` cells show an em dash (@sec:printing explains how to change the
text), so a pink background plus the dash is hard to miss.

## Rules for the whole table {#sec:style-css}

`lt_css()` is the home for everything that is not a one-off. It attaches CSS that
is emitted after the built-in stylesheet, so your rules win ties.

A **named** argument is an inline rule: the name is a selector, the value is
either a CSS string or a list of properties. Rules are scoped to the table, so
`.good` really means `.lt-table .good`. In a list, property names can be written
in camelCase as in `lt_style()`.

```{r}
lt(head(mtcars[, 1:3], 5)) |>
  lt_style(~ mpg, test = "v => v >= 21", class = "good") |>
  lt_css(
    .good = list(color = "darkgreen", fontWeight = "bold"),
    "tbody tr:hover" = "background: #f4f8ff",
    "th" = "text-transform: uppercase; font-size: .8em"
  )
```

An **unnamed** argument is a stylesheet: a path or a URL. Use it when the rules
live in a file you maintain, such as a house style shared by every table in a
report. Paths stay as written, so a relative one remains portable.

```r
lt(d) |> lt_css("company-tables.css")
```

If a page holds many tables with the same `lt_css()`, the stylesheet is emitted
once, not once per table.

### The selectors worth knowing {#sec:style-selectors}

Every part of a table has a class, so you can restyle anything without guessing
at the structure. @tab:style-selectors lists the ones you will reach for most.

:::: {.table #tab:style-selectors}
::: caption
[ ](#@tab:style-selectors) CSS selectors for the parts of an lt table.
:::

| Part | Selector |
|:-----|:---------|
| The table | `.lt-table` |
| Title, subtitle | `.lt-title`, `.lt-subtitle` (inside `caption.lt-caption`) |
| Column spanners | `.lt-spanner` |
| Row group labels | `.lt-row-group` |
| Indented stub cells | `.lt-indent` |
| Footer rows | `.lt-footer`, `.lt-footnote`, `.lt-source-note` |
| Footnote marks | `.lt-fnref` |
| Right/center aligned cells | `.al-r`, `.al-c` |
| Column type labels | `.lt-type` |
::::

The table is an ordinary HTML table, so `thead th`, `tbody td`, and
`tr:nth-child(odd)` all work too.

## Keep it on one table {#sec:wrap}

Page-wide CSS is great until the page has two tables. `lt_wrap()` solves that by
putting attributes on the `<div>` that wraps the table. Give it a `class`, and a
stylesheet rule that begins with that class touches this table only.

```{r, child = ex('css-wrap')}
```

The wrapper takes any HTML attribute, not only `class`. A fixed width and an
`id` for deep links are the usual suspects:

```{r}
lt(head(mtcars[, 1:4], 3)) |>
  lt_wrap(id = "cars", style = "max-width: 28em")
```

Repeated calls accumulate classes instead of replacing them, so a helper
function can add its own class without wiping the caller's.

## Peek behind the format {#sec:style-raw}

One last trick needs no code. **Alt-click** on a table to reveal the *raw* value
behind every cell that was formatted: `0.0012` appears next to `0.001`, and an
ISO timestamp next to its friendly date. **Alt-double-click** does the same for
every table on the page. It is a cheap way to check that a format hides noise
and not information.
